title: Making nettle liquid feed
subtitle: A nitrogen-rich brew from young nettle stems and water.
excerpt: Nettle liquid feed is a nitrogen-rich plant feed brewed from young nettle stems steeped in water. Ready in two to four weeks, it supports leafy growth in brassicas, salad crops, and established perennials.
sourceNotes: Nitrogen content of nettle tissue from published horticultural chemistry data. Brewing method after organic kitchen gardening guides widely available in the UK. Harvest timing from seasonal plant growth observations.

glossaryTerms.definition: A plant feed high in nitrogen (N), which supports leafy, vegetative growth. Used on brassicas, salad crops, lawns, and any plant where leaf production is the goal rather than flowers or fruit.

content.text: brewed from young nettle stems and water. It supports leafy growth and suits brassicas, salad crops, and any plant you are growing primarily for its leaves. The brew smells unpleasant but costs nothing if you have nettles at the garden edge.
Young stems cut before the plant flowers make the strongest feed. A two-week brew in warm weather gives a usable concentrate; four weeks gives a stronger result.

Cut the top 30 cm of young nettle stems from April to July, before the plant flowers. Wear thick gloves. Cut from an area well away from roadsides and anywhere that may have been treated with herbicide. Wash the cut stems briefly.

Pack the cut stems into a bucket. Add water to cover, then weigh the stems down so they stay submerged. Cover loosely with a lid or sacking. Leave in a warm spot for two to four weeks, stirring once or twice a week if you can.
After two weeks the stems have mostly broken down and the liquid is dark brown. Strain the liquid into bottles. The remaining plant matter goes on the compost heap.

Dilute 1:10 with water before applying. The diluted feed should look pale brown. Apply around the base of leafy crops every two weeks through the growing season. Use it for brassica transplants a week after planting, once they have settled in. It is too high in nitrogen for fruiting crops such as tomatoes and courgettes, where potassium is more useful during the cropping period.

attrs.title: Mixing with comfrey
attrs.body: A half-and-half mix of nettle feed and comfrey feed gives a more balanced plant feed with both nitrogen for leafy growth and potassium for flower and fruit. Use this blend on courgettes, squash, and cucumbers through the season, switching to comfrey-only once the first fruits set.

content.text: A 10-litre bucket packed with stems and topped up with water yields roughly 7 to 8 litres of concentrate after straining. Diluted 1:10, that is 70 to 80 litres of ready-to-use feed. A nettle patch 1 m square provides enough material for two or three batches per season.
